title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Which particle has a relative mass of approximately $\dfrac{1}{1836}$?
questions.solution:
The **electron**. Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of about 1.

Almost all an atom's mass is in the nucleus, and almost all its **volume** is the electron cloud.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: The electron configuration of a calcium atom ($Z = 20$) is:
questions.solution:
$4s$ fills **before** $3d$, because it is slightly lower in energy at that point.

That inversion is why the transition metals begin at scandium rather than immediately after argon — and why they lose their $4s$ electrons first when ionised.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: The first ionisation energy generally increases across a period because:
questions.solution:
Across a period, protons are added while the outer electrons all enter the **same shell**, so the shielding hardly changes.

The effective nuclear charge rises, the atom contracts, and the outer electron is held more firmly.

The small **dips** at Al and at S are what reveal the sub-shell structure.
options: the nuclear charge increases with little extra shielding

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Two isotopes of an element differ in:
questions.solution:
Isotopes differ only in **neutrons**.

Their chemistry is essentially identical, since that depends on the electrons — but their physical properties differ slightly, which is how they can be separated in a mass spectrometer.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Across Period 3 from Na to Ar, the atomic radius:
questions.solution:
It **decreases**. The nuclear charge grows while the electrons enter the same shell, so the whole shell is pulled in more tightly.

**Down a group** the radius increases instead, because an entire new shell is added each time.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: An element has isotopes of mass $10$ ($20\%$) and $11$ ($80\%$). Find its relative atomic mass.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: How many electrons can a d sub-shell hold?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{10}$ — five orbitals, each holding two electrons of opposite spin.

s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.

questions.q: How many neutrons are in an atom of $^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}$?

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: How many unpaired electrons are in a nitrogen atom ($Z = 7$)?
questions.solution:
$1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{3}$ — the three $2p$ electrons occupy the three $2p$ orbitals **singly**, by Hund's rule.

$\mathbf{3}$ unpaired, which is why nitrogen forms three bonds.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Find the oxidation number of chlorine in $\text{HClO}_{4}$.
questions.solution: $+1 + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+7}$ — the maximum for chlorine, and it makes perchloric acid a very strong oxidising agent.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Define first ionisation energy, explain the trend across Period 3 including the two anomalies, and explain how successive ionisation energies reveal the group of an element.
questions.solution:
**Definition.** The energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms:

$\text{X}(g) \to \text{X}^{+}(g) + e^{-}$

The word **gaseous** matters — otherwise lattice or intermolecular energies would be involved.

**The general trend across Period 3: it increases.** The nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons stay in the same shell, so shielding hardly changes, the effective nuclear charge grows and the atom contracts.

**Anomaly 1: Al is lower than Mg.**

Magnesium's outer electron is in $3s$; aluminium's is in $3p$, which is **higher in energy** and better shielded by the filled $3s$. It is therefore easier to remove.

**Anomaly 2: S is lower than P.**

Phosphorus is $3p^{3}$, with three singly occupied orbitals. Sulphur is $3p^{4}$, so one orbital holds a **pair**, and the mutual repulsion between them makes one electron easier to remove.

**These two dips are strong evidence for sub-shells and for Hund's rule** — nothing in a simple shell model predicts them.

**Successive ionisation energies.** Each is larger than the last, since the electron is being pulled from an increasingly positive ion.

But there is a **large jump** whenever a new inner shell is broached. The number of electrons removed **before** that jump is the number of outer electrons — and therefore the group.

For magnesium the jump comes after the second, so magnesium is in Group 2. It is a direct experimental route to electronic structure.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Describe how a mass spectrometer determines the relative atomic mass of an element, and calculate $A_{r}$ for an element with peaks at $24$ ($79\%$), $25$ ($10\%$) and $26$ ($11\%$).
questions.solution:
**The stages.**

1. **Vaporisation** — the sample must be gaseous.

2. **Ionisation** — bombardment with high-energy electrons knocks an electron off each atom, giving $\text{X}^{+}$. Only charged particles can be manipulated by fields.

3. **Acceleration** — an electric field gives all the ions the same kinetic energy, so the lighter ones travel faster.

4. **Deflection** — a magnetic field bends the beam. The radius depends on $\dfrac{m}{z}$: **lighter ions are deflected more**.

5. **Detection** — the ions arriving produce a current proportional to their abundance.

**The output** is a spectrum with one peak per isotope, its position giving the mass and its height the relative abundance.

**The calculation:**

$A_{r} = \dfrac{(79 \times 24) + (10 \times 25) + (11 \times 26)}{100}$

$= \dfrac{1896 + 250 + 286}{100} = \dfrac{2432}{100} = \mathbf{24.32}$

This is **magnesium**.

**A check on any such answer:** it must lie between the lightest and heaviest isotope, and nearest the most abundant. $24.32$ is just above 24, as an $79\%$ abundance of mass 24 requires ✓

**Its other uses:** identifying unknown compounds from their fragmentation pattern, radiocarbon dating, and detecting drugs in athletes' samples.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Describe and explain the trends across Period 3 in atomic radius, melting point and the acid-base nature of the oxides.
questions.solution:
**Atomic radius — decreases across the period.**

Nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons remain in the same shell, so shielding is nearly constant and the effective nuclear charge pulls the shell in.

**Melting point — a striking pattern in three parts.**

• **Na, Mg, Al:** metallic lattices, and the melting point **rises** as each atom contributes more delocalised electrons and the ion charge increases.

• **Si:** a giant covalent lattice, with the **highest melting point of all** — every bond must be broken to melt it.

• **P, S, Cl, Ar:** simple molecules ($\text{P}_{4}$, $\text{S}_{8}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}$) held by weak van der Waals forces, so the melting points are **low**.

Among these, $\text{S}_{8}$ melts highest because it is the largest molecule with the strongest dispersion forces.

**The oxides — basic to acidic across the period.**

• $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$ — **ionic and basic**; they react with acids and, for sodium oxide, dissolve to give an alkali.

• $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ — **amphoteric**, reacting with both acids and alkalis. The turning point.

• $\text{SiO}_{2}$, $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_{2}$, $\text{SO}_{3}$ — **covalent and acidic**; they dissolve to give acids.

**The single explanation behind all three trends:** the change from **metallic** to **covalent** bonding as the electronegativity difference with oxygen falls. Metals give electrons away and form ionic, basic oxides; non-metals share them and form covalent, acidic ones.

Aluminium sits exactly on the boundary, which is why its oxide answers to both.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: State the rules governing the filling of orbitals, and write the configurations of Cr, Cu and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, explaining the anomalies.
questions.solution:
**The three rules.**

1. **Aufbau principle** — orbitals fill from the lowest energy upwards.

2. **Pauli exclusion principle** — an orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins.

3. **Hund's rule** — electrons occupy degenerate orbitals **singly**, with parallel spins, before any pairing begins. Pairing costs energy through mutual repulsion.

**Chromium ($Z = 24$).** Expected $[\text{Ar}]3d^{4}4s^{2}$; actual $\mathbf{[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}}$.

**Copper ($Z = 29$).** Expected $[\text{Ar}]3d^{9}4s^{2}$; actual $\mathbf{[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}}$.

**Why.** The $3d$ and $4s$ levels are extremely close in energy, and a **half-filled or completely filled** $d$ sub-shell is unusually stable — the electrons are as far apart as possible, minimising repulsion.

Promoting one $4s$ electron costs very little and gains that stability, so it is worth doing.

**$\text{Fe}^{3+}$.** Iron is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{6}4s^{2}$.

**The $4s$ electrons are removed first**, even though $4s$ filled first — once $3d$ is occupied, it drops below $4s$ in energy.

So $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $\mathbf{[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}}$ — a half-filled $d$ sub-shell, which is exactly why $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is more stable in solution than $\text{Fe}^{2+}$.

'Fill $4s$ first, empty it first' is worth remembering as a single rule.

questions.chapter: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Define electronegativity, describe how it varies across a period and down a group, and explain what it predicts about bonding.
questions.solution:
**Definition.** The ability of an atom to **attract the bonding pair of electrons** in a covalent bond towards itself.

The Pauling scale runs from about $0.7$ (caesium) to $4.0$ (fluorine, the most electronegative element).

**Across a period: increases.** The nuclear charge rises while the atomic radius falls, so the nucleus pulls the bonding pair more strongly.

**Down a group: decreases.** The bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so the attraction weakens.

**The most electronegative elements** are therefore at the **top right**: F, O, N, Cl.

**What it predicts.**

• **Zero difference** — a pure **covalent** bond, with the pair shared equally ($\text{H}_{2}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}$).

• **Small difference** — a **polar covalent** bond, with partial charges $\delta+$ and $\delta-$ (H–Cl).

• **Large difference** (above about $1.7$) — **ionic** bonding, with the electron effectively transferred (NaCl).

**It is a continuum, not three separate categories** — bonds shade gradually from one type to the next.

**What polarity leads to.** Polar bonds may give a polar **molecule**, and hence dipole-dipole forces, higher boiling points, and solubility in water.

But a symmetrical molecule cancels its own bond dipoles: $\text{CO}_{2}$ has two very polar bonds and **no** overall dipole, while the bent $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ molecule does — which is why one is a gas and the other a liquid.

**And where H is bonded to N, O or F**, the polarity is extreme enough for **hydrogen bonding**, which dominates the chemistry of water, alcohols, proteins and DNA.
